description: Conducting an authorised penetration test end to end: rules of engagement and the law, open-source and active reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation and password attacks, post-exploitation and privilege escalation, and reporting findings with remediation. Practised only against isolated virtual machines and simulated networks in the browser, with every exercise scoped and authorised so techniques are learned lawfully.
modelledOn: Weidman, Penetration Testing: A Hands-On Introduction to Hacking
Engebretson, The Basics of Hacking and Penetration Testing
OWASP Testing Guide and NIST SP 800-115
outcomes: Scope an engagement and work within rules of engagement, authorisation and the relevant law.
Gather intelligence on a target with open-source and active reconnaissance.
Scan and enumerate hosts, services and versions to build an attack surface map.
Exploit vulnerabilities and crack passwords against authorised lab targets.
Escalate privilege, move laterally and establish persistence during post-exploitation.
Write a clear penetration test report that prioritises findings and recommends remediation.

units.title: Rules of engagement and the law
topics: Why authorisation is everything: the line between a penetration test and a crime
Ghana's Cybersecurity Act 2020 and Data Protection Act 843; the Cyber Security Authority and lawful disclosure
Scoping: targets, exclusions, time windows, permitted techniques and emergency contacts
Rules of engagement, get-out-of-jail letters, data handling and confidentiality
Penetration testing methodologies and standards; types of test: black, grey and white box
Professional ethics and responsible disclosure

units.title: The tester's environment
topics: Building an isolated lab of virtual machines and a simulated network in the browser
A testing distribution and its toolchain; keeping test traffic off production
Note-taking, evidence capture and command logging for a defensible report
Networking refresher: addressing, ports, protocols and the OSI layers as they matter to testing

units.title: Reconnaissance
topics: Passive open-source intelligence: WHOIS, DNS records, certificate transparency, search and social media
Footprinting an organisation: employees, technologies, leaked credentials and metadata
Active reconnaissance and when passive crosses into active
Mapping the external attack surface, including exposed mobile-money and SIM-registration portals
Organising findings into a target profile

units.title: Scanning and enumeration
topics: Host discovery and port scanning with nmap; scan types, timing and evasion basics
Service and version detection and operating-system fingerprinting
Vulnerability scanning with OpenVAS and interpreting results without over-trusting them
Enumerating services: web, SMB, SNMP, SMTP, DNS and databases
Turning scan output into a prioritised list of likely entry points

units.title: Exploitation
topics: From vulnerability to working exploit; matching a service version to a known flaw and CVE/CVSS
Using an exploitation framework: payloads, listeners and sessions
Common server-side flaws: unpatched services, default credentials, misconfigurations
Client-side and social-engineering vectors in a controlled lab
Verifying impact without damaging the target; avoiding denial of service

units.title: Password attacks
topics: Where credentials live: hashes, caches, configuration files and memory
Online attacks: brute force, dictionary, spraying and credential stuffing against lab services
Offline cracking of captured hashes with John the Ripper and hashcat; wordlists and rules
Default and reused passwords; the weakness of SMS one-time codes and SIM-swap risk
Defences: strong hashing, lockout, multi-factor authentication

units.title: Post-exploitation
topics: Local situational awareness after a foothold: users, processes, network and stored secrets
Privilege escalation on Linux and Windows: misconfigurations, weak permissions, kernel and service flaws
Lateral movement and pivoting through a simulated internal network
Persistence, and the difference between a test artefact and real-world stealth
Collecting proof of access and cleaning up afterwards

units.title: Web and network attack techniques
topics: Web application testing against the OWASP Top Ten: injection, broken authentication, access control
Intercepting proxies and request manipulation with Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP
Network attacks in the lab: sniffing, spoofing and man-in-the-middle
Wireless assessment basics against a simulated access point

units.title: Reporting findings
topics: Structure of a penetration test report: executive summary, methodology, findings, evidence
Rating severity with likelihood and impact; CVSS as an input, not the whole story
Writing actionable remediation that a stretched IT team in a cafe or school can apply
Re-testing and verifying fixes; the debrief
Capstone: a full authorised test of a simulated small-business network and a written report

schedule.title: Authorisation, law and scoping
schedule.exercise: Read a short scenario of a student who scans a bank website without permission, and write which laws apply, what authorisation would have been needed and how to disclose properly.

tasks.title: Decide, for eight requests from a client, which are inside an authorised test and which cross the line into a crime, and justify each
Draft a scope statement for a small clinic network listing targets, exclusions, time windows and emergency contacts, scored against a scoping rubric
Handle a case where a tester finds patient records exposed during a test, choosing lawful steps for stopping, reporting and data handling

schedule.title: Rules of engagement, methodology and ethics
schedule.exercise: Write a one-page rules-of-engagement document for testing a school network, covering permitted techniques, data handling and who to call if something breaks.

tasks.title: Complete a rules-of-engagement and authorisation letter for a test, picking the correct clauses from a list and spotting two missing ones
Match the type of test (black, grey, white box) to five client situations and explain what information each tester would start with
Respond to a vulnerability found in a stranger's website outside any engagement, choosing a responsible-disclosure path and scored on a rubric

schedule.title: Lab setup, evidence and networking refresher
schedule.exercise: Describe how you would keep test traffic off a production network and what you would record in your notes for each action.

tasks.title: Create an isolated lab of three virtual machines on a host-only network and verify that they reach each other but not the internet
Record a short testing session with command logging and timestamps, then write notes that let another tester repeat each step exactly
Capture traffic between two lab hosts, identify protocol, ports and flags for a TCP handshake and an HTTP request, and map each to its OSI layer

schedule.title: Reconnaissance and the attack surface
schedule.exercise: Build a target profile for a fictional company from supplied public information, ranking the most promising entry points with reasons.

tasks.title: Use passive lookups to list the DNS records, name servers and certificate names of a lab domain without touching the target
Sort a pile of public findings (staff names, job adverts, a leaked password list, file metadata) into useful and irrelevant for a profile and justify the choices
Map the external attack surface of a fictional mobile-money agent portal, flag three exposed assets and rate each by risk

schedule.title: Scanning and vulnerability assessment
schedule.exercise: Explain, using a worked example, why a scanner finding is a lead to verify rather than proof of a vulnerability.

tasks.title: Run a host discovery scan and a TCP port scan against a lab subnet and list the open ports and services for each live host
Detect service versions and operating systems on four lab hosts and note which published advisories apply to each version
Run a vulnerability scan, rank the results, and identify two results that turn out, on manual review, to be incorrect

schedule.title: Service enumeration and entry points
schedule.exercise: Write a prioritised list of five likely entry points from a given scan report and explain the reasoning behind the ranking.

tasks.title: Enumerate a lab web server, file share and DNS server and list the users, shares and records you can obtain without any credentials
Query an SNMP-enabled lab router with its default read-only string and list the interface and routing information it discloses
Rank the findings from three combined scan reports into a prioritised entry-point list with likelihood and effort, scored on a rubric

schedule.title: Matching flaws to fixes
schedule.exercise: Read the published advisory for a given lab service version and explain in plain language what the weakness is, what it would let someone do, and how to patch or configure it away.

tasks.title: Match a service version found on a lab host to its published advisory and record the affected versions and the recommended fix
Identify a lab service left with its vendor-default account enabled, record what it exposes, and write the one-line fix to remove the risk
Given a report naming a flawed lab service, decide in writing what evidence would prove impact without disrupting the service, and what you would not attempt

schedule.title: Scoping impact safely
schedule.exercise: Write the safety checks you would agree with a client before and after testing a fragile production-like service, so nothing is disrupted.

tasks.title: Design a safe phishing-awareness exercise for a small office, choosing the message, the recipients and the limits, and defend it to a rubric
Read a proof-of-access file left on a lab host to confirm a reported weakness, without changing any configuration, and log every command you ran
Decide whether to proceed, stop or ask the client at five points where testing a fragile service might cause an outage, and justify each decision

schedule.title: Credential weaknesses and defences
schedule.exercise: Compare five password policies by estimated strength and recommend one for a small bank, explaining the trade-off between security and usability.

tasks.title: List where credentials can be found on a lab host (configuration files, saved sessions, memory dumps) and explain the risk of each location
Test a lab login form against a short list of guessed passwords with lockout disabled, then re-test with lockout enabled and compare the outcome
Review a report that SMS one-time codes were bypassed by a SIM swap, and recommend stronger multi-factor options with their trade-offs

schedule.title: Post-foothold awareness and segmentation
schedule.exercise: Explain, from a given network diagram, how proper segmentation would have stopped a finding on one host from reaching a second, more sensitive host.

tasks.title: On a lab host reached during the test, list the logged-in users, running processes and listening ports, and note anything unexpected
Review a report describing a weak file permission that let a lab account gain higher privilege, and write the one configuration change that closes it
Trace, on a simulated internal network diagram, the path a compromised host could reach, and redesign the segmentation to block it

schedule.title: Reporting evidence and cleanup
schedule.exercise: Write the evidence-handling and cleanup checklist a tester should follow at the end of an engagement, including what must never be left behind.

tasks.title: Review a tester's end-of-engagement notes, confirm every test account and file was removed, and flag one item that was left behind
Explain, for three hypothetical findings, why a test artefact used to prove access is different from genuine persistence, and how each should be described in the report
Decide, for three hypothetical lab findings, whether each counts as a disclosed test artefact or undisclosed persistence, and how each should be written up

schedule.title: Web and network weaknesses in the lab
schedule.exercise: Pick three items from the OWASP Top Ten and explain, for a given lab web application, which class of weakness its symptoms best match.

tasks.title: Review a lab web application's responses for signs matching three OWASP Top Ten categories and record the evidence for each
Use an intercepting proxy to view and modify a single request to a lab web application, and record how the response changes
Capture traffic on a lab network segment and identify a plaintext credential, then propose the encryption fix that would have hidden it

schedule.title: Reporting and the capstone test
schedule.exercise: Write the executive summary and one finding of a penetration test report for a simulated small business, rating its severity and giving a remediation a small IT team could realistically apply.

tasks.title: Draft the structure of a penetration test report (summary, methodology, findings, evidence) for a given set of test notes
Rate three findings by likelihood and impact using CVSS as one input, and justify a severity that differs from the raw score with reasons
Lead a full authorised test of a simulated small-business network end to end and write the report, scored against a capstone rubric for scope, evidence and remediation
